finding.claim: Authorization bypass on file deletion. `require_allowed` is an alias for the boolean predicate `is_allowed`, not the aborting `ensure_allowed`. Its return value is discarded, so the 'delete' grant is never enforced. Any caller can delete any file.
finding.source: Any HTTP client sends DELETE /files/<fid> with any user identity, or none, and any known or guessable fid.
finding.sink: `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:19, the protected delete operation.

trace.note: `from acl import is_allowed as require_allowed` imports the non-aborting boolean function under a name that suggests enforcement.
The file is looked up by the attacker-supplied fid.
`require_allowed(g.user, f, "delete")` returns False but the result is ignored, so execution continues.
`is_allowed` only returns a bool and never calls abort(403).

finding.guards_checked: Checked acl.py: only `ensure_allowed` aborts, and delete_file does not use it. No other decorator or before_request hook enforces authorization. `load_user` only sets g.user and never rejects a request. Compare rename_file at views.py:26, which correctly uses ensure_allowed.

verdict.guard_found: none effective: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user from a header and never rejects; ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts but is not used in delete_file; require_allowed is the bool is_allowed with its result discarded.
verdict.reason: views.py:4 aliases the bool-returning acl.is_allowed (acl.py:4-5) as require_allowed, views.py:18 discards its result, and views.py:19 deletes unconditionally, so any anonymous caller who knows a valid fid can delete the file (rename_file at views.py:26 correctly uses ensure_allowed).

verdict_facts.guard_found: none effective: before_request load_user (views.py:10-12) only sets g.user; ensure_allowed aborts (acl.py:8-10) but is not used in delete_file
verdict_facts.reason: views.py:4 aliases the boolean is_allowed (acl.py:4-5, no abort) as require_allowed, and views.py:18 discards its result, so views.py:19 `del STORE[fid]` runs for any client, including anonymous ones, who know an existing fid.

finding.claim: Authentication is taken from a client-supplied HTTP header. `g.user` is set directly from `X-Session-User-Verified` with no session, signature or proxy-trust validation. Any client can impersonate any user, including a user who holds grants on a file. This defeats the ACL check on rename_file.
finding.sink: `ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "write")` at views.py:26 and the rename at views.py:27. The same identity would also be used in the delete check once F1 is fixed.

trace.note: The identity is used as the key into the grants dict.
`resource['grants'].get(user)` matches the spoofed name, so the check passes.

finding.guards_checked: There is no authentication middleware, token verification or session lookup in the code. The 'Verified' in the header name suggests an upstream proxy sets it. Nothing in this code strips the header from external requests, so the app is safe only if every request goes through a trusted proxy that overwrites it and the app is unreachable directly. That precondition is not enforced here.

verdict.guard_found: ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts 403 and is correctly used at views.py:26, but it only checks the spoofable g.user. There is no authentication, signature check or header stripping in the repo (only acl.py and views.py exist). Any upstream proxy that sets the header is outside this code.
verdict.reason: views.py:12 sets g.user straight from the client-controlled X-Session-User-Verified header, so an anonymous client can name any grantee and pass the check at acl.py:5/9 and the write at views.py:27. The only possible mitigation is an upstream proxy that overwrites the header, and nothing in this code enforces that.

verdict_facts.guard_found: Upstream trusted identity middleware (per maintainer facts). The header name `X-Session-User-Verified` implies a proxy sets it. In-directory, `ensure_allowed` at acl.py:9-10 aborts 403 when the grant is missing, and rename_file calls it at views.py:26.
verdict_facts.reason: The trace is accurate: views.py:12 reads the header and acl.py:5 matches it against the grants dict. The maintainer states that request identity such as g.user comes from trusted upstream middleware, so a header set by that layer is not attacker-controlled. The finding's own `guards_checked` says exploitability depends on an unverified proxy precondition outside this code, so it is not a defect here.
